quote: about 80% of training sessions are performed at low intensity (2 mM blood lactate), with about 20% dominated by periods of high-intensity work, such as interval training at approx. 90% VO2max
claim: Descriptive studies of nationally or internationally competitive endurance athletes converge on roughly 80% of sessions at low intensity (blood lactate about 2 mM) and about 20% of sessions containing high-intensity work such as intervals at about 90% VO2max.
number: 80% low-intensity sessions (~2 mM); 20% high-intensity sessions (~90% VO2max)
population: nationally or internationally competitive endurance athletes training 10-13 times per week
used_for: default session split (about 4 easy sessions for every hard session) in endurance plans
caveat: counts sessions, not minutes; describes what elite athletes do, not a tested optimum for recreational athletes

quote: high-volume, low-intensity exercise (HVLIT), usually performed below the first ventilatory threshold (VT1) or at stable lactate concentrations of ≤ 2 mM and referred to as “zone 1” intensity; (2) “threshold” training (THR) performed at or near the lactate threshold (LT ~4 mM) or second ventilatory threshold (VT2) and designated as “zone 2” intensity; (3) HIT in “zone 3” (≥4 mM)
claim: The research 3-zone model: zone 1 is below the first ventilatory threshold (VT1) or a stable lactate of about 2 mM or less; zone 2 is between VT1 and the second threshold (LT about 4 mM or VT2); zone 3 is above about 4 mM or VT2.
number: zone 1 <= 2 mM (below VT1); zone 2 up to ~4 mM (VT2); zone 3 >= 4 mM
population: endurance athletes (definitions used across TID research)
used_for: anchoring all zone schemes to the 3-zone model (LT1/VT1 and LT2/VT2)
caveat: fixed 2 and 4 mM values are population approximations; individual thresholds vary

quote: Zone 1 < 1.2 mM, 54–73% HRmaxZone2 1.3–2.0 mM, 74–83 HRmaxZone 3 2.1–3.6, 84–88 HRmaxZone 4 3.7–5.7 mM, 89–93 HRmaxZone 5 >5.8, >94% HRmax
claim: A 5-zone scale used with Norwegian elite cross-country skiers defined zone 1 as below 1.2 mM (54-73% HRmax), zone 2 as 1.3-2.0 mM (74-83% HRmax), zone 3 as 2.1-3.6 mM (84-88% HRmax), zone 4 as 3.7-5.7 mM (89-93% HRmax) and zone 5 as above 5.8 mM (above 94% HRmax). By lactate, 5-zone zones 1-2 fall in 3-zone zone 1, zone 3 in 3-zone zone 2, and zones 4-5 in 3-zone zone 3.
population: Olympic and world-champion Norwegian cross-country skiers and biathletes (Tonnessen et al. 2014, as tabulated in the review)
used_for: mapping 5-zone schemes onto the 3-zone model
caveat: the mapping to 3 zones is derived by comparing these lactate bands with the 2 and 4 mM anchors in END-02; %HRmax bands come from elite athletes and do not transfer reliably to individuals (see END-16)

quote: Findings indicate that elite endurance athletes spend a high percentage of their TID in a pyramid shape—that is, great portions of HVLIT with 84–95% in zone 1, 2–11% in zone 2, and 2–9% in zone 3
claim: In retrospective analyses of the preparation phase, elite endurance athletes trained mostly in a pyramidal distribution: 84-95% of training in zone 1, 2-11% in zone 2 and 2-9% in zone 3.
population: elite, nationally ranked to world-class rowers, runners, cyclists and cross-country skiers (preparation phase)
used_for: realistic time-in-zone targets for well-trained athletes
caveat: retrospective, mostly time-in-HR-zone; by time, the low-intensity share is higher than the session-based 80%

quote: The pooled results demonstrate a moderate effect (ES = -0.66; 95% CI: -1.17 to -0.15) favoring the POL group over the THR group.
claim: An early meta-analysis of randomised trials found a moderate effect on time-trial performance favouring polarized over threshold-focused training.
population: endurance-trained athletes with more than 2 years of training and VO2max above 50 ml/kg/min; 3 RCTs pooled
used_for: polarized versus threshold training debate
caveat: only 3 small trials with PEDro scores of 4-5/10

quote: Pooled effect estimates suggest POL superiority for improving VO2peak (SMD = 0.24 [95% CI 0.01, 0.48] ... Superiority, however, only occurred in shorter interventions (< 12 weeks) ... TT (SMD = – 0.01 [95% CI -0.28, 0.25]
claim: Polarized training improved VO2peak slightly more than other distributions (small effect), but only in interventions shorter than 12 weeks (and in highly trained athletes); time-trial performance did not differ.
number: VO2peak SMD 0.24 (0.01 to 0.48); only < 12 weeks; TT SMD -0.01 (-0.28 to 0.25)
population: 17 studies, 437 adult and young adult athletes
used_for: polarized versus other distributions
caveat: the authors could not separate the effect of training level from intervention length

quote: Based on the time in heart rate zone approach, there was no difference in VO2max (SMD = - 0.06, p = 0.68) or TT performance (SMD = - 0.05, p = 0.34) between POL and pyramidal (PYR) interventions.
claim: An individual-participant network meta-analysis found no difference between polarized and pyramidal distributions in VO2max or time-trial performance, and no significant difference between polarized and any other distribution.
population: 13 studies, 348 recreational and competitive endurance athletes (296 men, 52 women)
used_for: choosing a training intensity distribution
caveat: most interventions were short; few women

quote: Competitive athletes may have greater improvements to VO2max with POL, while recreational athletes may improve more with a PYR TID.
claim: In a subgroup analysis, competitive athletes appeared to improve VO2max more with polarized training, while recreational athletes improved more with a pyramidal distribution.
population: recreational (n = 150) and competitive (n = 198) endurance athletes
used_for: default distribution for recreational athletes (pyramidal) versus competitive athletes (polarized phases)
caveat: subgroup finding, hypothesis-generating

quote: no other TID model showed a definite advantage for improving ... or TT performance, because all 95% credible intervals crossed zero
claim: A 2026 Bayesian network meta-analysis found no model with a definite advantage over polarized training for VO2max or time-trial performance; threshold and HIT models only ranked highest by probability.
population: randomised trials in endurance athletes
used_for: choosing a training intensity distribution
caveat: rankings are probabilistic; abstract only

quote: Improvements were 5.0% vs 3.6%, ~41 s difference at post-training-intervention. This difference was not significant.
claim: In recreational runners, 10 weeks of polarized training (about 77/3/20) and between-threshold training (about 46/35/19) both improved 10-km time (5.0% vs 3.6%); the difference was not significant.
population: 30 recreational runners, 10 weeks, HR-guided zones from a lab test
used_for: intensity distribution for recreational runners
caveat: a subset analysis of the most compliant runners favoured polarized training

quote: Focused Endurance Training obtains similar improvements than Polarized Endurance Training saving 17% of training time in recreational runners.
claim: In recreational runners over 8 weeks, a threshold-focused plan (40/50/10) produced similar improvements to a polarized plan (77/3/20) with matched training load, using 17% less training time.
population: 38 recreational runners, 8 weeks, TRIMP-matched
used_for: time-limited recreational runners: more zone 2 work is a valid option
caveat: short study; matched by TRIMP rather than time

quote: prescribing exercise intensity based on a fixed percentage of these maximal anchors has little merit for eliciting distinct or domain-specific homeostatic perturbations
claim: Prescribing intensity as a fixed percentage of maximal anchors (VO2max, HRmax, maximal power or speed) does not reliably place individuals in the same intensity domain.
population: healthy adults and athletes (critical review)
used_for: preferring threshold-anchored zones over %HRmax zones
caveat: narrative review

quote: There is some evidence to support the validity of LT1, GET, and VT to delineate the moderate and heavy domains of exercise. However, there is little evidence to support the validity of most commonly used methods, with exception of CP and CS, to delineate the heavy and severe domains of exercise.
claim: LT1, the gas exchange threshold and VT1 have some support for marking the moderate-heavy boundary; for the heavy-severe boundary only critical power and critical speed have good support.
population: healthy adults and athletes (critical review)
used_for: choosing threshold anchors for zones
caveat: narrative review

quote: Equivocal stage of the TT, RPE of 10-11, and FS ratings between fairly good (+ 1) and good (+ 3) are reflective of the ventilatory threshold, while negative stage of the TT, RPE of 13-15, and FS ratings around neutral (0) are reflective of the respiratory compensation threshold.
claim: Without lab tests, the first threshold corresponds to the equivocal stage of the talk test (speech starts to become uncomfortable) and RPE about 10-11; the second threshold corresponds to the negative talk-test stage (comfortable speech not possible) and RPE about 13-15.
number: RPE 10-11 at VT1; RPE 13-15 at the respiratory compensation threshold
population: healthy adults and athletes (critical review)
used_for: RPE and talk-test zones for beginners and anyone without lab thresholds
caveat: RPE values imply the Borg 6-20 scale (not stated in the abstract); the review rates talk test and RPE as valid for both thresholds

quote: A regression equation to predict HRmax is 208 - 0.7 x age in healthy adults.
claim: Predicted maximal heart rate for healthy adults is 208 - 0.7 x age; the older 220 - age equation underestimates HRmax in older adults.
population: meta-analysis of 351 studies (18,712 subjects) plus a lab study of 514 healthy adults
used_for: HRmax estimate when no measured value exists
caveat: group-level equation; individual error is large (END-16)

quote: HRmax was univariately explained by the formula 211 - 0.64·age (SEE, 10.8) ... a standard error of 10.8 beats/min must be taken into account
claim: In 3320 healthy adults, HRmax was best predicted by 211 - 0.64 x age, with a standard error of estimate of 10.8 beats/min, so an individual's true HRmax can easily differ from any age formula by 10-20 beats/min.
population: 3320 healthy Norwegian men and women of a wide age range (HUNT Fitness Study)
used_for: warning that age-predicted HRmax zones can be off by a full zone
caveat: the 10-20 beats/min range is an interpretation of 1-2 standard errors

quote: In conclusion, %HRR should not be considered equivalent to %VO2max. Rather, %HRR is equivalent to %VO2R, and this relationship should be used in exercise prescription.
claim: Percent heart-rate reserve corresponds to percent VO2 reserve, not to percent VO2max; this is why %HRR (Karvonen) prescriptions account for resting heart rate and fitness better than %HRmax.
population: 63 adults, cycle ergometer tests
used_for: choosing %HRR over %HRmax when only heart-rate anchors are available
caveat: still a maximal-anchor method (END-12); the second sentence of the claim is an interpretation

quote: methodological differences in the assessment of these parameters typically result in MLSS occurring at a somewhat lower power output or running speed and exercise at CP being sustainable for no more than approximately 20–30 min
claim: Critical power (CP) or critical speed (CS) marks the boundary between the heavy and severe domains; it sits slightly above the maximal lactate steady state and can be sustained for only about 20-30 min, so it is not the same as a 60-min threshold.
population: healthy and trained adults (narrative review)
used_for: defining the top of zone 2 (heavy domain) and interpreting threshold tests
caveat: narrative review; MLSS and CP are measured differently and should not be treated as interchangeable

quote: CS may correspond to 95–99% of the speed of the longest trial length used ... It is recommended that testing protocols include: (1) at least three maximal effort trials of different durations performed in the severe domain ... (2) a shorter effort trial approximately 3 min in duration ... and (3) a longer effort approximately 15 min in duration
claim: To estimate critical speed, use at least three maximal efforts of different durations, including one of about 3 min and one of about 15 min; CS typically lies at about 95-99% of the speed of the longest trial.
number: 3 min and 15 min efforts; CS ~95-99% of longest-trial speed
population: runners (scoping review of 124 studies)
used_for: field test or race-result based critical speed for running pace zones
caveat: CS estimates shift with the trial durations chosen, so keep the protocol constant for re-tests

quote: These recommendations should be extended to CS and D′ estimates modelled from elite athlete-race data, whereby events ≤ 800 m and ≥ 10 km should not be included as a predictive trial.
claim: When estimating critical speed from race results, use races longer than 800 m and shorter than 10 km (for example 1500 m to 5 km); exclude 800 m and shorter and 10 km and longer.
population: runners (scoping review)
used_for: pace zones from race results
caveat: recommendation framed for elite race data; slower runners take longer over the same distance, so check that the efforts lasted roughly 3-15 min

quote: Across all studies, T1 occurred at 82.3% of CS (95% CI, 81.1-83.6).
claim: The first threshold (moderate-heavy boundary) occurs on average at about 82% of critical speed, slightly lower (about 81%) in slower runners and higher (about 83-84%) in faster runners.
population: 26 studies, 527 runners
used_for: estimating the top of zone 1 (easy running) from critical speed without lab testing
caveat: the authors note uncertainty from inconsistent threshold methods and recommend testing for precise work

quote: Runners completed the marathon at 84.8% ± 13.6% CS ... (93.0% CS for 150 min marathon times vs 78.9% CS for 360 min marathon times). Runners who completed the first half of the marathon at >94% of their CS ... were more likely to slowdown by more than 25% in the second half of race.
claim: Critical speed estimated from training data predicted marathon pace: recreational runners raced at about 85% of CS on average (93% for 2:30 finishers, 79% for 6:00 finishers); starting the first half above 94% of CS made a slowdown of more than 25% more likely.
population: >25,000 recreational marathon runners with GPS training data before big-city marathons
used_for: marathon and long-race pacing targets from CS; flagging over-ambitious race plans
caveat: observational; CS here was computed from best efforts over 400-5000 m in training logs

quote: Bland-Altman plots between FTP20, FTP60 and IAT showed small bias (-1 to -5 W), but large limits of agreement ([-40 to 32 W] to [-62 to 60 W]). Time to exhaustion at FTP20 was 50.9±15.7 min.
claim: FTP from 95% of a 20-min test (FTP20) agreed with 60-min power and a lab threshold on average, but individual limits of agreement were wide (roughly plus or minus 40-60 W), and cyclists could hold FTP20 for only about 51 min, not 60.
number: bias -1 to -5 W; LoA -40 to 32 W up to -62 to 60 W; TTE 50.9±15.7 min
population: 23 trained male cyclists
used_for: FTP test validity for individual zone setting
caveat: small sample of men

quote: the PO at MLSS representing 88.5% (4.8%) and 93.1% (5.1%) of FTP and FTP95%, respectively
claim: Power at the maximal lactate steady state was about 88.5% of 20-min test power and 93% of FTP (95% rule), so FTP overestimated MLSS, and FTP did not track the MLSS improvement after 7 months of training.
number: MLSS = 88.5% of FTP (twenty-minute power) and 93.1% of FTP95%
population: 18 well-trained men and women; 10 re-tested after 7 months
used_for: FTP test validity; caution with FTP-based threshold sessions
caveat: small sample

quote: FTP presented a bias ± 95% LoA of 1.4% ± 9.2%, a moderate TEE (4.7%), and nearly perfect correlation (r = .91) with MLSS in all cyclists together.
claim: In trained and well-trained cyclists, FTP (95% of 20-min power) estimated MLSS with a small bias (1.4%) but 95% limits of agreement of about plus or minus 9%; the authors judged it a practical alternative.
population: 15 trained and well-trained cyclists (VO2max about 62 ml/kg/min)
used_for: FTP test validity (supportive side)
caveat: agreement was worse in the less-trained group

quote: The FTP20 test was reported as a reliable test. Studies investigating the relationship of FTP20 with other physiological markers and power-related concepts reported large limits of agreement suggesting parameters cannot be used interchangeably.
claim: The 20-min FTP test is reliable (repeatable) but is not interchangeable with lab thresholds or critical power because of large limits of agreement; most evidence comes from trained male cyclists.
population: 15 studies, mostly trained male cyclists
used_for: how to use FTP: as a repeatable performance marker, not as an exact threshold
caveat: scoping review

quote: (4.9 mL·kg(-1)·min(-1); ... (5.5 mL·kg(-1)·min(-1); ... When compared with endurance training, there was a possibly small beneficial effect for HIT (1.2 mL·kg(-1)·min(-1); ±0.9 mL·kg(-1)·min(-1))
claim: In healthy young to middle-aged adults, both continuous endurance training (+4.9 ml/kg/min) and high-intensity interval training (+5.5 ml/kg/min) produced large VO2max gains versus no exercise; HIT gave a possibly small extra benefit (+1.2 ml/kg/min).
number: ET +4.9; HIT +5.5; HIT vs ET +1.2 ±0.9 mL/kg/min
population: 28 controlled trials, 723 healthy adults aged 18-45 (mean 25 years)
used_for: choosing HIIT or continuous training for general fitness
caveat: magnitude-based inference statistics

quote: significantly increases CRF in adults compared to non-exercise control (standardized mean difference [SMD]: 0.28 to 4.31; weighted mean difference [WMD]: 3.25 to 5.5 mL/kg/min) and MICT (SMD: 0.18 to 0.99; WMD: 0.52 to 3.76 mL/kg/min)
claim: An umbrella review found HIIT improves cardiorespiratory fitness versus no exercise (3.25-5.5 ml/kg/min) and versus moderate continuous training (0.52-3.76 ml/kg/min) across healthy, overweight, older and athletic adults.
number: vs control WMD 3.25-5.5 mL/kg/min; vs MICT WMD 0.52-3.76 mL/kg/min
population: 24 meta-analyses, 429 primary studies, 12,967 adults
used_for: time-efficient cardio for time-limited people
caveat: most included reviews had moderate to critically low AMSTAR-2 quality

quote: the gain in VO2max was significantly greater following interval training (MD = 1.10; CI = 0.55-1.64)
claim: In middle-aged and older adults, interval training raised VO2max about 1.1 ml/kg/min more than moderate continuous training.
population: 14 studies, 429 middle-aged and older adults
used_for: cardio for the sedentary 45-year-old once a base is established
caveat: small absolute difference; both modes work

quote: The incidence of RRI was 20.8% in the graded training program group and 20.3% in the standard training program group.
claim: In a randomised trial, a 13-week programme following the 10% rule did not reduce running injuries compared with a standard 8-week programme for novice runners (20.8% vs 20.3%).
population: 532 novice runners preparing for a 6.7-km event
used_for: the 10% rule is not protective on its own
caveat: both programmes were low volume and started with run-walk

quote: consisted of three training sessions ... were advised to run at a comfortable pace at which they could converse without breathlessness. ... The program started 8 weeks before the start of the Groningen four mile run at the level of a run-walk session with a total of 10 minutes of running and 10 minutes of walking
claim: The GRONORUN beginner programmes used three run-walk sessions per week at a conversational pace, starting with 10 minutes of running and 10 minutes of walking per session (week 1: ten repeats of 1 min running and 1 min walking), building to continuous running for a 6.7-km event.
number: 8 weeks; 10 min running + 10 min walking per session
population: novice runners aged 18-65 without recent lower-limb injury (trial design paper)
used_for: concrete starting point for beginner run-walk plans
caveat: the 1 min/1 min structure is from the programme table; both programmes had about 20% injury incidence (END-30)

quote: (hazard ratio = 1.59; 95% confidence interval: 0.96, 2.66; P = .07). ... Novice runners who progressed their running distance by more than 30% over a 2-week period seem to be more vulnerable to distance-related injuries
claim: Novice runners who increased weekly distance by more than 30% over 2 weeks tended to have more distance-related injuries (such as patellofemoral pain, IT band and shin problems) than those increasing by less than 10%; the result was not statistically significant.
number: more than 30% over 2 weeks; HR 1.59 (95% CI 0.96-2.66)
population: 874 novice runners with GPS watches, 1-year cohort
used_for: upper limit for weekly progression in beginners
caveat: exploratory; no difference in total injury rate across progression groups

quote: Significantly increased rates were identified for small spikes (HRR=1.64 (95% CI: 1.31 to 2.05, p=0.01)), moderate spikes (HRR=1.52 (95% CI: 1.16 to 2.00, p<0.01)) and large spikes (HRR=2.28 (95% CI: 1.50 to 3.48, p<0.01)) in single-session running distance. A negative dose-response relationship was observed for the ACWR. No relationship was identified for the week-to-week ratio.
claim: A single run longer than the longest run of the previous 30 days raised overuse-injury rate: by 64% for a 10-30% spike, 52% for 30-100% and 128% for more than 100%; weekly spikes (week-to-week ratio or ACWR) were not associated with higher injury rates.
population: 5205 adult runners (mean age 45.8, 22% women), 18-month Garmin cohort
used_for: long-run progression rule; questions the weekly 10% rule
caveat: observational; self-reported injury

quote: Runners should avoid running a distance in their current session that exceeds 10% of the longest distance covered in the previous 30 days. However, progressions up to 10% are not necessarily safe either and carry a degree of risk.
claim: Keep any single run within 10% of the longest run completed in the previous 30 days; even increases under 10% carry some risk.
number: 10% of the longest run in the previous 30 days
population: 5205 adult runners (cohort)
used_for: long-run progression in all running plans
caveat: single cohort study; mostly men from Europe and North America

quote: The meta-analyses revealed a weighted injury incidence of 17.8 (95% confidence interval [CI] 16.7-19.1) in novice runners and 7.7 (95% CI 6.9-8.7) in recreational runners.
claim: Novice runners had about 18 running-related injuries per 1000 h of running versus about 8 per 1000 h in recreational runners, so beginners need the most conservative progression.
population: 13 prospective studies of novice and recreational runners
used_for: risk framing for beginner runners
caveat: heterogeneous injury definitions

quote: average weekly running distance, number of weekly runs, maximum running distance completed in a single week, number of runs ≥32km completed in the pre-marathon training block, average running pace during training, distance of the longest run and hours of running per week ... identified a negative statistical association between each of the above listed training behaviours and marathon performance (R2 0.38-0.81, p<0.001)
claim: Across marathon cohorts, higher weekly distance, more runs per week, a higher peak week, more runs of 32 km or longer, a longer longest run and more weekly hours were each associated with faster marathon times.
population: 85 studies, 137 cohorts of elite and recreational marathon runners (25% women)
used_for: what to build in marathon and ultra preparation: frequency, volume, long runs
caveat: between-cohort associations from observational data; not dose prescriptions and not causal

quote: Average training distances in adult UER are between 66 and 83 km/week
claim: Adult ultra-endurance runners typically train about 66-83 km per week on average.
population: adult ultramarathon runners (studies cited in an expert narrative review)
used_for: plausibility check for ultra plan volume
caveat: descriptive averages of experienced ultrarunners, not a minimum for a first 50 km

quote: one of the clearest effects of endurance exercise is on the cardiovascular system, including right ventricular dysfunction and potential increased risk of arrhythmias and hypertension. There is also evidence that rare cases of acute renal injury in UER could lead to progressive renal scarring and chronic kidney disease.
claim: Possible long-term risks of repeated ultra-endurance running include right ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias and hypertension, and rare acute kidney injury that might progress; women, youth and masters athletes may be more susceptible.
population: ultra-endurance runners (expert narrative review)
used_for: health counselling and referral thresholds for ultra athletes
caveat: mostly low-quality and cross-sectional evidence; serious acute events are rare

quote: most (64.6%) reported an exercise-related injury that resulted in lost training days (median of 14 days) ... Prior year incidence of stress fractures was 5.5% with most (44.5%) involving the foot. Ultramarathon runners who sustained exercise-related injuries were younger (p<0.001) and less experienced (p<0.01) than those without injury.
claim: Among active ultramarathon runners, 64.6% had an injury costing training days in the previous year (median 14 days); 5.5% had a stress fracture, most often in the foot; younger and less experienced ultrarunners were more often injured, and stress fractures were more common in women.
population: 1212 active ultramarathon runners (median age 42, 68% men, mostly USA), self-reported
used_for: injury risk framing for first-time ultra runners
caveat: retrospective self-report

quote: Mean race intensity was 77.1%±4.4% of HRmax distributed as: 85.7%±19.4% Zone I, 13.9%±18.6% Zone II, 0.4%±0.9% Zone III.
claim: In a 65-km mountain ultra (4000 m climbing), amateur trail runners averaged 77% of HRmax and spent about 86% of race time below VT1; the authors propose VT1 as the boundary of tolerable intensity for such events.
number: 77.1% HRmax; 85.7% zone I; 13.9% zone II; 0.4% zone III
population: 23 amateur trail runners, 65-km mountain ultra
used_for: ultra race intensity and specificity of zone 1 training
caveat: one race, small sample

quote: Current scientific evidence shows that prior exposure to DR is the most effective strategy to limit the magnitude of EIMD as a result of the so called “repeated bout effect”.
claim: Prior exposure to downhill running is the most effective way to limit muscle damage from downhill running (repeated bout effect).
population: healthy and trained adults in lab and field studies (narrative review)
used_for: downhill conditioning in trail and ultra preparation
caveat: narrative review; mostly lab protocols

quote: Byrnes et al. [193] showed that the RBE procured by a prior 30 min DR disappeared after 9 weeks with no eccentric muscle actions between the first and second bout.
claim: The protection from one 30-min downhill run was gone after 9 weeks without eccentric loading, so downhill exposure must be repeated within the build, not only early in the plan.
population: single study cited in the review
used_for: timing of downhill sessions before a trail race
caveat: the practical conclusion about scheduling is an inference

quote: It is well-reported that MVC force/torque is impaired for several days following DR (up to 4–5 days for a complete recovery; see Fig. 1).
claim: Maximal strength stays reduced for several days after strenuous downhill running, with full recovery taking up to 4-5 days.
population: healthy adults in downhill running studies (narrative review)
used_for: spacing hard downhill sessions from key workouts and races
caveat: depends on slope, duration and prior exposure

quote: DOMS recorded after a 45-min DR bout was lower following a short DR training (five training sessions in 1 week; duration: 5–15 min; slope: − 10%
claim: Short downhill training (five sessions in one week of 5-15 min at a -10% slope) reduced soreness after a later 45-min downhill run; two weeks of training protected more than one.
number: 5 sessions in 1 week; 5-15 min; -10% slope; 45 min
population: healthy adults (Schwane et al., cited in the review)
used_for: dose for introducing downhill running
caveat: lab treadmill study in non-runners; 'two weeks protected more' is from the same paragraph, not the quote

quote: Follow up back-to-back workouts with at least two easy days. ... While there is some debate on the efficacy of back-to-back long runs ... try doing back-to-back long runs twice before your ultra. A good rule of thumb is 30 to 40 miles over two days for a 50K
claim: Practitioner advice: back-to-back long runs are standard but debated ultra practice; do them about twice before a first ultra, about 30-40 miles (about 48-64 km) over two days for a 50 km, followed by at least two easy days.
number: 30 to 40 miles over two days for a 50K
number_note: 48-64 km is a unit conversion of 30-40 miles
population: recreational ultrarunners (coach opinion)
used_for: back-to-back long runs in a 50 km ultra plan
caveat: practitioner opinion without research evidence; combine with the single-session spike rule (END-34)

quote: It increased on positive slopes, attained 17.33 +/- 1.11 J. kg(-1). m(-1) at +0.45 ... Cr was 3.40 +/- 0.24 J. kg(-1). m(-1) on the level, independent of speed. It increased on positive slopes, attained 18.93 +/- 1.74 J. kg(-1). m(-1) at +0.45, and was reduced to 1.73 +/- 0.36 J. kg(-1). m(-1) at -0.20.
claim: The energy cost of running per metre rises from 3.40 J/kg/m on the flat to 18.93 at a +45% grade (more than 5 times) and falls to 1.73 at -20%; at +45% walking (17.33) costs less than running, so pace on trails must be interpreted against grade.
population: 10 runners on a treadmill
used_for: interpreting trail pace versus grade; power-hiking steep climbs
caveat: small lab study

quote: Heat acclimatisation sessions should last at least 60 min/day, and induce an increase in body core and skin temperatures, as well as stimulate sweating. ... Early adaptations are obtained within the first few days, but the main physiological adaptations are not complete until ∼1 week. Ideally, the heat acclimatisation period should pass 2 weeks in order to maximise all benefits.
claim: Athletes racing in the heat should heat-acclimatise with sessions of at least 60 min per day that raise core and skin temperature and cause sweating; main adaptations take about 1 week and the full benefit about 2 weeks.
population: athletes preparing to train and compete in hot conditions
used_for: heat preparation in endurance plans (for example a hot ultra)
caveat: heat illness recognition and emergencies belong to SAF; fluids to NUT

quote: the rate of decay of heat acclimatisation is generally slower than its induction, allowing maintenance of the majority of benefits (eg, heart rate, core temperature) for 2–4 weeks
claim: Most heat-acclimatisation benefits are maintained for 2-4 weeks, so a heat block can end up to a few weeks before the race.
population: athletes (consensus statement)
used_for: timing a heat block within a race build
caveat: decay of actual race performance is less clear

quote: Cardiovascular drift, the progressive increase in heart rate and decrease in stroke volume that begins after approximately 10 min of prolonged moderate-intensity exercise, is associated with decreased maximal oxygen uptake, particularly during heat stress. Consequently, the increased heart rate reflects an increased relative metabolic intensity
claim: Heart rate drifts upward from about 10 min into prolonged moderate exercise, especially in the heat; this rise reflects a real increase in relative intensity, so holding heart rate constant (slowing down) during long sessions in heat is appropriate.
population: healthy adults exercising in heat (narrative review)
used_for: interpreting HR drift in Strava/Garmin data; pacing long runs and rides by HR
caveat: the pacing advice is an inference from the review

quote: The optimal strategy to optimize performance is a tapering intervention of 2-wk duration (overall effect = 0.59 +/- 0.33, P < 0.001), where the training volume is exponentially decreased by 41-60% (overall effect = 0.72 +/- 0.36, P < 0.001), without any modification of either training intensity
claim: The most effective taper lasted about 2 weeks, with training volume reduced progressively by 41-60% while intensity and frequency were kept.
population: 27 studies of competitive athletes
used_for: taper design before key races
caveat: older meta-analysis; frequency kept is also in the abstract

quote: The tapering applied in conjunction with pre-taper overload training seems to be more conducive to maximize performance gains. Current evidence suggests that a ≤21-day taper, in which training volume is progressively reduced by 41–60% without changing training intensity or frequency, is an effective tapering strategy.
claim: In endurance athletes, a taper of up to 21 days with volume progressively reduced by 41-60% and unchanged intensity and frequency is effective, and works best after a period of overload training.
population: 14 studies of endurance athletes
used_for: taper design; placing the hardest block just before the taper
caveat: few studies per subgroup

quote: strict 3-week tapers were associated with superior marathon finish-time benefits (a median finish-time saving of 5 min 32.4 s or 2.6%) compared with a minimal taper
claim: Among recreational marathoners, a disciplined 3-week taper (volume falling each week) was associated with a median finish-time benefit of 5.5 min (2.6%) compared with a minimal taper.
population: >158,000 recreational marathon runners (training data)
used_for: taper length for marathon and longer races
caveat: observational; most runners (64%) used less disciplined tapers

quote: Running economy (RE) was measured in 20 of the studies and generally showed improvements (2-8%) compared to a control group ... The addition of two to three ST sessions per week, which include a variety of ST modalities are likely to provide benefits to the performance of middle- and long-distance runners.
claim: Adding strength training (heavy, explosive or plyometric) generally improved running economy by 2-8%; two to three strength sessions per week with varied modalities are likely to benefit distance runners, without harming body composition.
population: 24 studies of middle- and long-distance runners with at least 6 months of experience
used_for: strength sessions in runners' plans
caveat: inconsistent across studies; PEDro 4-6

quote: it is therefore recommended that a recovery period of > 3 h is provided following high-intensity running training before ST takes place
claim: When strength training and hard running fall on the same day, allow more than 3 hours after the high-intensity run before the strength session.
population: distance runners (systematic review recommendation)
used_for: scheduling strength and running sessions in the weekly plan
caveat: many studies put strength on separate days

quote: High load and combined training methods induced moderate (effect size = - 0.469, p = 0.029) and large effect (effect size = - 1.035, p = 0.036) on running performance, respectively. While plyometric training was not found to have a significant effect
claim: High-load strength training (at least 80% 1RM) had a moderate effect and combined methods a large effect on running time-trial performance, while plyometrics alone was not significant; none improved VO2max.
population: middle- and long-distance runners (324 moderately trained, 272 well trained, 298 highly trained)
used_for: type of strength work for runners
caveat: certainty of evidence very low to moderate

quote: Running economy is improved by performing combined endurance training with either heavy or explosive strength training. However, heavy strength training is recommended for improving cycling economy.
claim: For runners both heavy and explosive strength training improve running economy; for cyclists heavy strength training is recommended and has the most compelling evidence of improving cycling performance.
population: endurance-trained runners and cyclists (narrative review)
used_for: strength training for cyclists
caveat: narrative review

quote: endurance performance can be maintained for up to 15 weeks when training frequency is reduced to as little as 2 sessions per week or when exercise volume is reduced by 33-66% (as low as 13-26 minutes per session), as long as exercise intensity (exercising heart rate) is maintained
claim: Endurance performance was maintained for up to 15 weeks when frequency fell to as little as 2 sessions per week, or when volume was cut by 33-66% (as low as 13-26 minutes per session), provided exercise intensity (heart rate) was kept.
number: up to 15 weeks; 2 sessions per week; 33-66% volume reduction; 13-26 min per session
population: general populations (narrative review of mostly short studies)
used_for: maintenance during busy periods; time-limited clients
caveat: narrative review; insufficient data for athletes

quote: Overall, evidence about the association between weekly running distance, duration, frequency, intensity, or specific changes in training parameters and the onset of RRIs was conflicting.
claim: A systematic review of prospective studies found conflicting evidence linking weekly running distance, duration, frequency, intensity or recent changes in these to running-related injuries, and cautions against recommending optimal parameters or progressions.
population: 23047 runners in 36 prospective studies
used_for: running volume progression
caveat: observational studies with different definitions of injury and exposure

quote: The incidence of RRI was 14.9% in novice runners (range = 9.4%-94.9%), 26.1% in recreational runners (range = 17.9%-79.3%), and 62.6% in competitive runners (range = 52.6%-91.3%). The 3 most frequently injured body parts were the knee (25.8%), foot/ankle (24.4%), and lower leg (24.4%).
claim: Running-related injury incidence was 14.9% in novice, 26.1% in recreational and 62.6% in competitive runners; the knee (25.8%), foot/ankle (24.4%) and lower leg (24.4%) were the most often injured sites.
number: novice 14.9%; recreational 26.1%; competitive 62.6%; knee 25.8%; foot/ankle 24.4%; lower leg 24.4%
population: runners in 36 prospective studies
used_for: injury expectations
caveat: very wide ranges between studies (for example 9.4%-94.9% in novices)

quote: All equations used in this study show poor agreement between measured HRmax and APMHR. The Fox equation may represent the best option for a general population as it is less likely to under or overestimate based on individual HRmax. Individuals should use data from GXTs to determine HRmax when applicable to ensure accuracy.
claim: In 99 adults tested on a treadmill, all nine age-based HRmax equations agreed poorly with measured HRmax; the authors recommend a measured maximal test where possible and suggest the Fox equation is the least likely to under- or overestimate across individuals.
population: 99 adults from a general population, maximal treadmill tests
used_for: HRmax estimation
caveat: one single-site study; the paper's discussion, not END-15, defines the equations compared

quote: Significant differences between measured and predicted HRmax were found for the Gulati, Astrand, Nes, and Fairbarn (male) equations (p < 0.05). Bland-Altman plots revealed wide limits of agreement for all nine APMHR equations, suggesting poor agreement between measured and predicted HRmax.
claim: Average predicted HRmax differed significantly from measured HRmax for the Gulati, Astrand, Nes and male Fairbarn equations, and all nine equations had wide limits of agreement for individuals.
population: 99 adults from a general population
used_for: HRmax estimation
caveat: do not rely on any single equation for an individual; check zones against RPE and the talk test

quote: The time to task failure at FTP and FTP+15W were 33.7 ± 7.6 and 22.0 ± 5.7 minutes (p < 0.001), respectively.
claim: Cyclists reached task failure after about 33.7 minutes (SD 7.6) when riding at FTP, not 60 minutes, and after about 22.0 minutes (SD 5.7) at 15 W above FTP.
number: 33.7 ± 7.6 min at FTP; 22.0 ± 5.7 min at FTP+15 W
population: 13 cyclists, constant-power rides to task failure
used_for: FTP validity
caveat: small sample of trained cyclists

quote: The VO2 response corresponding to FTP and FTP+15W suggests that FTP should not be considered a threshold marker between heavy and severe intensity.
claim: From the oxygen-uptake and lactate responses at and just above FTP, the authors conclude that FTP is not a valid marker of the boundary between heavy and severe intensity.
population: 13 cyclists
used_for: FTP validity

quote: No evidence is currently available favoring a specific periodization model during 8 to 12 weeks in trained road cyclists. However, few studies have examined seasonal impact of different periodization models in a systematic way.
claim: In trained road cyclists, no periodization model (block, traditional or day-by-day) is favoured by current evidence over 8 to 12 weeks; seasonal comparisons are rare.
population: trained road cyclists, 7 studies
used_for: cycling periodization
caveat: few and heterogeneous studies

quote: Training volume ranged from 8.75 to 11.68 h·wk-1 and both pyramidal and polarized TID were used.
claim: In the block-periodization studies of trained road cyclists, weekly training volume ranged from 8.75 to 11.68 hours, with both pyramidal and polarized intensity distributions.
population: trained road cyclists in block-periodization studies
used_for: cycling volume reference
caveat: descriptive; not a recommended dose

quote: comfortable speech is likely possible (equivocal or last positive talk test stage) when exercise intensity is below the ventilatory or lactate threshold, and not likely possible (negative talk test stage) when exercise intensity exceeds the ventilatory or lactate threshold.
claim: In healthy adults and cardiac patients, comfortable speech is likely possible below the ventilatory or lactate threshold and not possible above it, which is the basis for using the talk test to set and monitor intensity.
population: healthy adults, competitive athletes and patients with cardiovascular disease (narrative review)
used_for: talk test
caveat: narrative review

quote: The talk test has been shown to be consistent across various modes of exercise (i.e., walking, jogging, cycling, elliptical trainer and stair stepper). It may not be practical for high-intensity interval training.
claim: The talk test gave consistent results across walking, jogging, cycling, elliptical and stair-stepper exercise, but it may not be practical for high-intensity intervals.
population: healthy adults and patients with cardiovascular disease (narrative review)
used_for: talk test
caveat: use RPE or power or pace for interval sessions

quote: Previous experience (e.g., number of finishes in ultra-marathon races and personal best marathon time) is the most important predictor variable for a successful ultra-marathon performance followed by specific anthropometric (e.g., low body mass index, BMI, and low body fat) and training (e.g., high volume and running speed during training) characteristics.
claim: Ultra-marathon performance is predicted most by previous experience (number of ultra finishes, marathon personal best), then by anthropometric characteristics and training volume and speed; this is association data, not a training prescription.
population: ultra-marathon runners (narrative overview)
used_for: ultra preparation
caveat: associations, not causal

quote: Ultra-marathoners are older and have a larger weekly training volume, but run more slowly during training compared to marathoners.
claim: Ultra-marathoners train with larger weekly volume but run more slowly in training than marathoners.
population: ultra-marathoners compared with marathoners (narrative overview)
used_for: ultra preparation
caveat: does not give a km-per-week target

quote: In longer ultra-marathons, ~50-60% of the participants experience musculoskeletal problems. The most common injuries in ultra-marathoners involve the lower limb, such as the ankle and the knee.
claim: In longer ultra-marathons about 50-60% of participants experience musculoskeletal problems during the race, most often in the lower limb (ankle and knee).
population: participants of longer ultra-marathons (narrative overview)
used_for: ultra injury expectations
